desc:
Two nodes of a binary tree are cousins when they are on the same depth (the root has depth 0) but have different parents. Siblings (same parent) are not cousins.

Given the tree and two different values x and y, both of which occur in the tree, return true if the nodes holding them are cousins, otherwise false.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, -1, 4, -1, 5], nodes 4 and 5 are cousins (both on depth 2, parents 2 and 3), so x = 4, y = 5 gives true. Nodes 2 and 3 are siblings, so x = 2, y = 3 gives false.
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
x != y, and both values occur in the tree
hints: Two facts decide the answer for each of the two nodes: how deep it is and who its parent is.
Because values are distinct, you can store, for every value, a pair (depth, parent value) while walking the tree.

With the array encoding, the k-th real node owns the child slots 2k+1 and 2k+2. One left-to-right pass can therefore record depth and parent of every node; the answer is depth[x] == depth[y] and parent[x] != parent[y].
editorial: Walk the tree once (level by level, or recursively) and remember for each node its depth and its parent. Then compare: equal depth and different parent means cousins. A breadth-first search can also stop as soon as it finishes the level on which one of the two values is found: if the other is on that same level with a different parent the answer is true, otherwise false.

Every node is visited once, so the time is linear. The array encoding lets you do it without building node objects: real nodes come in level order, and the children of the k-th real node sit at slots 2k+1 and 2k+2 of the array.
